question: How many sequences of \(0\)s and \(1\)s of length \(19\) are there that begin with a \(0,\) end with a \(0,\) contain no two consecutive \(0\)s, and contain no three consecutive \(1\)s?
solution:
Because the sequence begins and ends with \(0\), every run of \(1\)s lies between two successive zeros. Each such gap must contain exactly one or two \(1\)s: an empty gap would create \(00\), and a longer run would contain \(111\).

Suppose there are \(z\) zeros. There are \(z-1\) gaps and \(19-z\) ones, so
\[
z-1\le19-z\le2(z-1).
\]
The first inequality gives \(z\le10\), and the second gives \(z\ge7\). Thus the only possibilities are \(z=7,8,9,10\).

Place one \(1\) in each gap first. Together with the zeros, this uses \(2z-1\) symbols. To reach length \(19\), exactly
\[
19-(2z-1)=20-2z
\]
gaps must receive one additional \(1\). Choosing those gaps determines the entire sequence. Conversely, every valid sequence uniquely identifies its chosen gaps, so this counts each sequence exactly once.

The four disjoint cases give
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{Zeros} & \text{Gaps} & \text{Gaps with two ones} & \text{Count}\\ \hline
10&9&0&\binom{9}{0}=1\\
9&8&2&\binom{8}{2}=28\\
8&7&4&\binom{7}{4}=35\\
7&6&6&\binom{6}{6}=1
\end{array}
\]
Here \(\binom82=8\cdot7/2=28\) and \(\binom74=(7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4)/(4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1)=35\). Adding the counts gives
\[
1+28+35+1=\boxed{65},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

reference.solution:
Method 1: Choose which gaps contain two ones

Because the sequence begins and ends with \(0\), every run of \(1\)s lies between two successive zeros. Each such gap must contain exactly one or two \(1\)s: an empty gap would create \(00\), and a longer run would contain \(111\).

\text{Zeros} & \text{Gaps} & \text{Gaps with two ones} & \text{Count}\\ \hline
10&9&0&\binom{9}{0}=1\\

edges.reason: Outcome enumeration provides concrete practice partitioning and counting finite outcomes. Probability ratios are unnecessary, as Gemini notes, but that does not erase the useful enumeration component.
Systematic pair listing practices completeness and avoiding double counts. Its multiplication structure is not needed to add disjoint category sizes, so keep the broad counting preparation only.
edges.scope: systematic counting without repetition or omission

edges.reason: Dividing ordered counts by internal permutations supplies a standard derivation. Evaluating the supplied factorial quotient or a Pascal recurrence does not require first computing a permutation number.
C(n,k) evaluates an unordered selection count; the combination concept gives the object and its non-order-sensitive meaning.
Single-valued correspondence helps formalize the encoding and its inverse. However, elementary bijective counting can work through informal one-to-one pairing without set-theoretic function language.
